messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 64
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Jeweler
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Male Presence: Being alone with men, Conflict: Confrontations
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Miguel Alvarez is a 64-year-old jeweler who came to treatment after years of feeling that he was never fully safe, even in the small workshop he has run for decades. He grew up in a Spanish-speaking household where, as a boy, he repeatedly witnessed his father assault his mother during explosive arguments. What stayed with him were not long narratives but a series of hard, fixed images: his father’s face red with shouting, his mother cornered near the kitchen table, a belt in his father’s hand, the glint of metal objects on the counter that suddenly looked like weapons. Even now, when those memories come, they arrive as vivid snapshots rather than a flowing story, each scene painfully clear. With the memories comes a rush of guilt that he should have done something, and from that guilt he has come to believe he failed in the role that mattered most, that he was weak, and that over the years he drifted away from the sense of belonging and cultural closeness he once associated with family and community.

Those old scenes continue to shape what catches his attention in the present. In his shop, where he spends long hours alone with customers and repair tools, a man raising his voice over a price dispute or even speaking sharply across the counter can bring back those same frozen images with startling force. Being alone with male customers is especially difficult; if a confrontation seems possible, Miguel feels himself tense before anything has happened. Because the memories are so clear and guilt-laden, he tries hard not to think about them, and he closely monitors his own mind for signs that he is “losing it” whenever an image intrudes. He has also stopped letting himself relax, even during quiet afternoons at the bench, because lowering his guard feels dangerous, as if that would be the moment something bad would happen.

Over time, these efforts to control his inner experience have narrowed his life. When he notices himself becoming calm, he interrupts it by scanning his thoughts and surroundings, and the more he does this, the more easily the old pictures return. He describes trying to push the memories away, only to have them come back sharper later, often tied to very specific cues: shouting from the sidewalk outside, two men arguing in the neighboring store, or the uneasy feeling of being shut in the shop with a man he does not know. He has begun arranging appointments to avoid being alone with male clients when possible, and he keeps interactions brief if a customer seems irritated. These habits make sense to him because he is certain that if he stops watching, he will miss the first sign of danger.

That sense of danger now colors nearly every environment. Miguel automatically notices tools, letter openers, hammers, and display rods as potential weapons; in a jeweler’s workspace, dangerous objects are everywhere, and he is aware of them the moment he enters the room. He watches other people closely for signs they might harm him, especially men, and when others reassure him that nothing is wrong, he cannot believe them. His belief that he is a weak man who once failed to protect someone important leaves him feeling that he cannot rely on himself now, which makes the world seem even less safe. In turn, living in this constant state of alertness deepens his shame. He sees himself as the kind of person who still has to scan every face and every hand, and that becomes further proof, in his mind, that something in him is deficient.

The triggers have also taken on personal meaning. A loud male voice does not register as only noise; it immediately evokes the old conclusion that he is again the powerless boy who could not stop what was happening. A confrontation with a customer can leave him preoccupied for hours, not just frightened but flooded with the sense that he has spent a lifetime failing at the central role of protecting others and standing firm. He speaks with sadness about how far he feels from the version of himself tied to family, church, and neighborhood life in his younger years; he keeps to himself now, and that isolation has come to feel like one more sign that he has lost his place in his community.

What finally brought Miguel in was an incident at work when two male customers began arguing loudly over a custom piece. He found himself staring not at their faces but at the metal tools on his bench and the movements of their hands. Afterward he could not settle, kept checking his thoughts for evidence he was breaking down, and spent the evening trying not to see the old kitchen scenes that nonetheless flashed back in precise images. He is seeking help now because he is tired of living as though violence is always about to break through the door. What frightens him most is that he will remain trapped in this vigilant, constricted life, unable to trust safety or himself; what he hopes for, though he says it cautiously, is to be able to work, rest, and be around other people without feeling that the past is waiting in every raised voice.
